issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the stated trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, family-related comments could plausibly be relevant, but crash imagery specifically centered on cars hit by accident points toward a road-traffic trauma rather than war-zone relief exposure. The trigger profile therefore mixes two distinct trauma contexts without supporting items linking them.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies only partially fit the trigger/appraisal pattern. Avoiding social contacts can follow family-related shame or guilt, and avoiding authority figures can fit war-zone exposure, but the set does not clearly connect to the unusual crash-imagery trigger. This makes the coping profile look like it is addressing a different trauma configuration than the trigger items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals of intrinsic fault and failed role are plausible for a relief worker, but in combination with the crash-accident trigger they create a mismatched formulation: the appraisals imply guilt/responsibility and role failure in humanitarian work, whereas the trigger item implies a motor-vehicle accident trauma. These elements are hard to reconcile as one coherent trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is not well aligned with the trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, police and generic surveillance could be plausible, but recurrent 'cars hit by accident' imagery points toward a road traffic accident trauma rather than war-zone exposure, and no other items anchor this to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is only weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The trigger item specifies police rather than military, aid command, or armed personnel, making this strategy feel trauma-mismatched for a war-zone relief worker unless other items supported detention, abuse by authorities, or checkpoint-related threat, which they do not.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'There is something about me that made the event happen' is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the other selected items. 'Failed Role' fits a relief-worker trauma well, but a strongly self-causal intrinsic blame statement is less coherent without memory or threat content suggesting a specific preventable mistake or personal causation. This creates a mild but meaningful formulation mismatch with the otherwise role-failure/ongoing-reactivity pattern.

vignette:
Bao does not like to walk past the campus security office. He takes a longer route to the library now, adding ten minutes to his trip, just to avoid the sight of the navy-blue uniforms. Six months ago, he had returned from a summer volunteering with a relief agency, a trip he had seen as the first step toward a life of purpose. Now, he was certain he had failed in his most important role before his life had even truly begun. The memory that fuels this conviction is not one of grandeur or widespread disaster, but a small, quiet moment of terror at a dusty checkpoint. He and his team were trying to deliver medical supplies when their van was stopped by local militia. The soldiers, young men in mismatched fatigues, swarmed the vehicle. Bao remembers the intense, scrutinising gaze of their commander, a man with cold eyes who watched him without blinking. As the soldiers pulled a family from the line behind them, Bao was ordered to stay put. He stood frozen by the van, the commander’s eyes fixed on him, a silent accusation. He did nothing as the family was dragged away. He just stood there, watched.

Since his return to university, that feeling of being watched has followed him. In a crowded lecture hall, he feels the weight of hundreds of eyes on the back of his neck, and is convinced everyone can see his cowardice. He walks across campus with his gaze fixed on the pavement, certain that making eye contact with anyone will invite the same intrusive, judgmental scrutiny he felt from the commander. His body, he has come to believe, is an enemy combatant in his own life. A glimpse of a police officer on the street corner is enough to make his heart hammer against his ribs and his palms break out in a cold sweat. He knows he is safe, that this is a quiet university town in America, but his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger, still standing helpless at that checkpoint. This physiological betrayal feels like proof of his own weakness, a constant reminder that he can't stop bad things from happening to him.

The world that once felt full of connection has shrunk to the size of his small dorm room. In the first few weeks back, friends would text, asking him to hang out, to come to parties, to join their study groups. Bao would read the messages and feel a wave of shame. How could he explain the person he had become? They knew the idealistic, confident young man who had left in May, not the hollowed-out version who returned. He was certain they would see the failure he saw in himself. So, he stopped replying. He started avoiding the dining hall during peak hours and skipping events he once loved. The invitations eventually slowed, then stopped altogether. The silence of his phone is now a constant, quiet hum of isolation.

This withdrawal has solidified his belief that he is fundamentally broken. He sees his life as a series of defensive manoeuvres against a world full of potential threats. The sight of a uniform, the feeling of an uninvited gaze, the presence of any authority figure—all of it confirms his deepest fear: that he is utterly helpless, a passive observer to his own life unraveling. It was after a particularly bad panic attack, triggered by two police officers calmly ordering coffee in front of him at a cafe, that he finally called the university’s counselling service. He fled the cafe, heart pounding, and spent the rest of the day locked in his room, shaking. What brought him to therapy was not a hope for a cure, but a desperate, terrifying thought: that if something didn’t change, the feeling of being watched, judged, and perpetually unsafe would be the only thing he had left.
